newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus, Turkey undermine US claim that crisis ended.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus, Turkey undermine US claim that crisis ended.

text.p: Cyprus dismissed talk of a deal to ease tension and Turkey renewed its warnings on Tuesday only hours after a U.S. peace envoy had announced a looming crisis between the two countries was over.

Cyprus said Carey Cavanaugh, who left on Monday talking of an imminent breakthrough on ways to reduce tension along the ceasefire line that separates Greek and Turkish Cypriots on the Mediterranean island, had misunderstood.
Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan followed with fresh warnings to Greece and the Cypriot government against a military buildup on Cyprus.
Cavanaugh had been sent to defuse a row over Cyprus's plan to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles. Cyprus says they are needed for self-defence, but Turkey calls them a threat.

Despite the reaction of Cyprus and Turkey, some observers thought he had eased tension by announcing after seeing Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides on Monday that the missiles would not be installed for 16 months.
"He reduced tension just by saying it was reduced," one Western diplomat in capital Nicosia said.
"The fact that the Americans have said the situation is defusing is enough. It may not show now but that view will soon make it to Turkey," he said.
But Erbakan renewed his calls for Cyprus to end plans to deploy the missiles, which have a range of 150 km (90 miles) and could reach Turkey.
"It is wrong to turn Cyprus into a barrel of gunpowder. I hope Greece and Greek Cyprus give up these intolerable provocations and get smart," Erbakan said.
The Cypriot government said the 16 month-period before deploying the missiles is enough to find a solution to the 23-year-old division of the island.
It has shrugged off Western criticism and Turkish threats, saying it needs missiles to protect Greek Cypriot areas of the island from Turkey, which occupies its northern third.
The Cypriot government dismissed Cavanaugh's assertion the two sides were close to a military agreement on ways to reduce tension along the ceasefire line.

"There has not been any agreement other than that which was already in place, that the military dialogue would continue based on what is stipulated in the relevant resolution of the United Nations," Clerides told reporters.

Yiannakis Cassoulides, Cypriot government spokesman, said: "President Clerides has reiterated to Mr Cavanaugh his intention to intervene in the military dialogue with our own military people and see what is happening with the dialogue and try to help it to advance. That's all."
The U.N. proposals relate to unloading weapons along the 180-km (110-mile) ceasefire line and abandonning sentry posts. They also impose a code of conduct on soldiers.

Diplomats said Cavanaugh's claim was reminiscent of a visit last year by U.S. Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright who announced talks between both sides military commanders, only for the plans to fall through after she left.
Four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot soldier have been killed in incidents along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone since June, raising tension.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has about 30,000 troops in the north while the internationally recognised Cypriot government has 11,500 in the south.
